title: Mertens' theorems
summary: Mertens (1874) proved $\sum_{p \le x} \frac{\log p}{p} = \log x + O(1)$, $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p = \log\log x + M + o(1)$, and $\prod_{p \le x}(1 - 1/p) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log x$, all without the prime number theorem.
why: These are the estimates sieve methods start from.
references: Montgomery & Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I
Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory

title: The prime number theorem
summary: $\pi(x) \sim x/\log x$, conjectured by Gauss and Legendre in the 1790s and proved in 1896 by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin. The key step is that $\zeta(1+it) \ne 0$.
why: The size of the error $\pi(x) - \operatorname{li}(x)$ is controlled by the zeros of $\zeta$.
references: Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory

title: Nontrivial zeros and the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula
summary: Zeros in the critical strip $0 < \operatorname{Re}s < 1$ are the nontrivial zeros. The number with $0 < \operatorname{Im} s \le T$ is $N(T) = \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e} + O(\log T)$. The first is $\tfrac12 + 14.134725\ldots\,i$.
why: Hardy (1914) showed infinitely many lie on the critical line.
references: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function

timeline.title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude
timeline.text: Continued $\zeta$ to the complex plane, proved the functional equation, linked zeros to primes and stated the Riemann hypothesis.

timeline.title: Infinitely many zeros on the critical line
timeline.text: Proved infinitely many zeros have real part $\tfrac12$.

title: The explicit formula
summary: Riemann's formula, proved by von Mangoldt in 1895, writes $\psi(x)$ exactly as a sum over the zeros $\rho$. A zero $\rho = \beta + i\gamma$ contributes a term of size $x^{\beta}$.
why: It is why every statement about zeros is a statement about primes.
references: Montgomery & Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I

title: Zero-free regions
summary: Regions near $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ with no zeros. De la Vallée Poussin (1899) found $\sigma > 1 - c/\log|t|$, and Vinogradov and Korobov (1958) a wider region, but in all of them the width shrinks to $0$ as $|t| \to \infty$. The classical proof uses $3 + 4\cos\theta + \cos 2\theta \ge 0$.
why: The width of the zero-free region is exactly the strength of the prime number theorem's error term.
references: Montgomery & Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I
Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function

title: Dirichlet characters
summary: Homomorphisms $\chi: (\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times \to \mathbb C^\times$, extended by $0$. There are $\varphi(q)$ of them, and orthogonality isolates a residue class. A character is primitive if it is not induced from a smaller modulus.
why: Characters are how one picks out primes in a single arithmetic progression.
references: Ireland & Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory

leads_to.title: Dirichlet L-functions and primes in progressions

title: Gauss sums
summary: $g(\chi) = \sum_{a \bmod q} \chi(a) e^{2\pi i a/q}$. For primitive $\chi$, $|g(\chi)| = \sqrt q$. For the quadratic character modulo a prime, $g^2 = \left(\frac{-1}{p}\right) p$, which gives a proof of quadratic reciprocity.
why: Gauss sums connect multiplicative characters to additive ones and appear in every functional equation of an $L$-function.
references: Ireland & Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory
